text:
There are movies that pass through you like weather and movies that take up residence in the conscience and refuse to leave. Kingdom of Heaven, seen as it was meant to be seen, belongs to the second order. It is not merely a crusader epic with dust and banners and the clang of steel. It is a meditation on what a man is for, what a city is worth, what peace costs, and what it means to keep your soul when kings, priests, armies, and history itself try to play you like a piece on a board. That is why it stands apart from the usual pageant of swords and slogans. Other films in its field sell you the thrill of belonging to a side. This one asks whether you can still be a man if the side is wrong, if the holy place is about to fall, if virtue is inconvenient, and if the only winning move left is to surrender the thing you were told to die for so that the living might walk out of the fire.

At its heart the story is simple enough to carry a life. A man leaves a small life in the West after grief has emptied it, follows a father he barely knew toward Jerusalem, and finds not a cartoon of glory but a fragile Christian kingdom holding the Holy City under a dying king while a vast invading power gathers to take it. You are not meant to leave with a tourist’s map of battles. You are meant to leave with a question that will not sit still. What man is a man who does not make the world better. That line is carved into wood before the journey even begins, and the whole film is the proving of it. The takeaway is not that war is pretty. The takeaway is that conscience is the last territory that cannot be occupied unless you hand over the keys.

Sit with the chess scene long enough and you will understand why people who have seen the film once still quote it years later as if it were scripture they found in a dusty chapel. The leper king, Baldwin, hidden behind silver, invites the young knight to sit. The whole world is in chess, he says. Any move can be the death of you. Do anything except remain where you started and you cannot be sure of your end. Then comes the sadness that gives the scene its true weight. When he was sixteen he won a great victory and felt in that moment he would live to be a hundred. Now he knows he will not see thirty. That is the lesson people miss when they treat the sequence as pretty dialogue. Victory does not cancel mortality. Glory does not bargain with the body. A crown does not stop the rot under the mask. The king who held a peace together, who understood that Jerusalem must welcome more than one people not only because it was expedient but because it was right, is already leaving the board. The sadness is not only that a good king is dying. The sadness is that the game continues after the only player who knew how to keep it from becoming slaughter is gone. A king may move a man, a father may claim a son, but that man can also move himself, and only then does he begin his own game. Your soul is in your keeping alone, even when those who presume to play you are kings or men of power. When you stand before God you cannot say you were told to do thus, or that virtue was not convenient at the time. This will not suffice. Remember that. The film is not whispering a slogan. It is placing the entire burden of adulthood on the table between two men and a board of carved pieces. If you take nothing else, take this. History will shove you. Commanders will order you. Faith will be shouted at you until your ears ring. None of that will serve as an alibi for the life you actually lived.

That is also why the crusaders, in the moral architecture of this story, are not a mob of faceless zealots. The film insists there is a difference between the men who came to safeguard the helpless and do no wrong, and the men who wore the same cross while lighting the fuse of disaster. Godfrey gives the charge like a baptism in steel. Be without fear in the face of your enemies. Safeguard the helpless. Do no wrong. That is the code the good men try to keep while an invading caliphate presses upon a kingdom already strained by disease, politics, and the hunger of holy ground. Baldwin is the philosopher king of that code, a Christian ruler who would rather punish the wicked in his own ranks than feed the war that would drown the city. When Reynald of Chatillon, the butcher among them, breaks the peace and treats massacre as piety, the king does not shrug and call it zeal. He makes the man kneel. He says he is Jerusalem. He demands the kiss of peace as if to drag a wolf back into the house of law. The point is not subtle and it is not fashionable. The film shows that a cause is not made righteous by the worst men who claim it. The bad in their ranks are named, shamed, constrained, and, when the old king still has breath, banished from the center of power. That is a lesson modern stories often refuse. It is easier to paint an entire host as either saints or monsters. Kingdom of Heaven will not grant that ease. It says the Holy City was held, for a little while, by men who understood that peace is a kind of courage, and that the first duty of a knight is not to feed the furnace but to keep the helpless from being thrown into it.

Then the good king dies, and the board is seized by men who prefer a war they can own. Guy and Reynald march pride into the desert and lose an army that should have guarded walls and wells and women and children. The invasion comes not as a debate club but as a tide. Jerusalem stands with too few knights and too many souls who cannot fight. Here the film becomes what most war pictures are afraid to be. It does not treat the city as a trophy that must be clutched until every last person is buried under stone. Balian knights ordinary men because nobility, in the hour of need, is not a bloodline. It is a willingness to stand between the helpless and the blade. He holds the walls not to feed a legend of invincibility but to force terms. That distinction is the moral spine of the climax. He is willing to surrender the Holy City to save the lives inside it. He threatens to burn the prizes that drive men mad, the holy places of both sides, not because he hates holiness but because he will not let holiness become an excuse for a graveyard. The invading commander offers safe conduct for every soul, the women, the children, the old, the knights, the queen. Then comes the question that has outlived reviews, box office, and fashion. What is Jerusalem worth. Nothing. Everything. That pair of words is the whole tragedy and the whole wisdom. The stones are not worth the innocent . The meaning men have poured into the stones has been worth empires, graves, and the bending of history. The lesson you are supposed to carry out of the theater is not that cities are cheap. It is that a man who confuses the idol with the innocent will burn the innocent to keep the idol. A man who knows the difference can lay the keys on the table and still have kept the kingdom that matters, the kingdom of conscience.

Watch it for that reason and it becomes a must watch rather than a handsome relic. Most historical epics want you drunk on belonging. This one wants you sober about responsibility. It stands out because it treats the crusader not only as a warrior but as a moral agent who can refuse both cowardice and fanaticism. It stands out because its finest Christian king is dying and still more alive in spirit than the healthy men who will wreck his peace. It stands out because the defense of Jerusalem is framed as a defense of people, not a defense of a slogan. It stands out because surrender, in the right hour, is shown as strength instead of stain. That is rare. Audiences are trained to cheer the last stand that produces a beautiful corpse. This film asks whether you would accept a living column of refugees over a magnificent ruin. If that question does not interest you, the picture will feel like a long march. If it does, the picture becomes a classic in the old sense, a work that keeps teaching after the spectacle has faded.

It is unique among its peers because it understands sadness as a form of knowledge. Baldwin’s chessboard is sad because a young victory already contains an early grave. Sibylla’s hidden grief, restored in the complete version, is sad because a mother can love a child and still have to face a crown that is also a sentence. The fall of the city is sad because the better order died before the walls did. The march away from Jerusalem is sad because the place was everything and nothing at once, a magnet for prayer and a magnet for blood. Yet the film will not let sadness become permission to stop being decent. That is the hard edge under the beauty. Pity without duty is just atmosphere. Duty without pity is how Reynald talks. The legend lives in the narrow road between them.

Call it a masterpiece when you mean the complete work, the long cut that restores breath, motive, and consequence. The theatrical version that first met the world was a wounded animal, hurried into summer like a second Gladiator and stripped of the very scenes that made its people human. Critics looked at the shortened body and said the film lacked depth, which is a remarkable diagnosis to offer a patient after you have removed the heart. In its finished form the film is deep because it lets a king test a knight’s mind as well as his sword arm, because it lets a woman be more than an ornament, because it lets common men receive knighthood as a moral promotion rather than a costume change, because it lets the defense of the city mean something before the stones start to fall. Production design the size of a vanished world, a score that moves like incense and iron, a masked performance of eerie gentleness, a desert that looks old enough to remember every army that ever lied about why it came, all of that would already be enough for admiration. What makes it an icon is that people still argue with it. They argue about the crusaders. They argue about the city. They argue about whether surrender was holy or weak. A film that is only pretty does not stay in the argument for twenty years. A film that tells you your soul is in your keeping alone will.

You watch it to learn that peace is not the absence of enemies. Peace is the presence of men willing to restrain their own. You watch it to learn that an invading host can be vast and still not dictate the terms of your character. You watch it to learn that the worst Christian in the story is not the proof against the best one. You watch it to learn that saving lives can be the last crusade left when the banners have become a trap. You watch it to learn that a blacksmith can become the defender of Jerusalem and then become a blacksmith again, which is another way of saying that greatness is a service, not a permanent costume. Richard of England will come looking for the legend and find a man who would rather tend a forge than feed another march. That ending is not a shrug. It is the film’s final act of sanity. After all the holy noise, someone has to go home and live.

The work behind the camera explains how a legend almost died in plain sight and then refused to stay dead. Ridley Scott built Jerusalem in the dust of Spain and Morocco, raised walls and courts and a city large enough to believe in, and trusted William Monahan’s language to carry philosophy through armor. Edward Norton played Baldwin as if royalty were a kind of suffering intelligence. Orlando Bloom’s Balian only makes full sense when the early grief is allowed to exist, when the murdered half brother and the mutilated wife and the carved Latin sentence are not treated as inconveniences. Eva Green’s Sibylla becomes tragic instead of decorative once the complete cut restores the child and the impossible choice attached to blood and crown. Liam Neeson’s Godfrey lasts just long enough to hand the code forward. Jeremy Irons watches a kingdom lose its mind with the bitterness of a man who saw the better road and could not make other men take it. Ghassan Massoud’s invading sovereign is written with ceremony and force, the face of a power that can offer terms or finish a city. Scott has said he cut what made the film meaty because preview nerves and studio appetite wanted speed. About forty five minutes walked out of theaters before the public ever sat down, including the darker family tragedy that gives the court its human cost. The result was a handsome confusion that earned mixed notices and a domestic shrug, then lived a second life on disc as one of the starkest proofs in modern cinema that editing can hide a great film inside a merely adequate one. The director’s cut runs like a roadshow of conscience, overture and all, and that is the version that earned the reputation the first release was denied. It is now common to hear that this is among Scott’s finest works, not because it is louder than Gladiator, but because it is wiser about what victory cannot buy.

If you come to it hunting only for a parade of Christian triumph, you will be disciplined by the ending. If you come hunting only for cynicism about faith, you will be disciplined by Baldwin, by the Hospitaler, by the knighting of men who had no titles, by the refusal to let the helpless be spent like coin. The film’s lasting power is that it will not let either appetite eat the whole plate. It says the crusader ideal, at its best, was to stand without fear, protect those who cannot protect themselves, and do no wrong, even when wrong would be useful. It says the men who betrayed that ideal from inside the walls were the ones who opened the road for catastrophe. It says an invading caliphate can take a city and still be answered by a defender . It says the saddest player on the chessboard may also be the wisest, and that wisdom does not get to stay. And it says, without mercy and without cheap comfort, that when the shouting is done you will not be able to hand your soul to a banner and call the account settled.

That is why it is a legend and a must watch. Not because every helmet is polished. Not because history has been freeze dried. Because it still does the rare thing art is for. It makes the Holy City feel heavy in your hands, then asks whether you love the people in it more than you love the argument about it. It makes a masked king more vivid than a thousand unmasked ranters. It makes surrender look like the last clean act available to a man who refused to become a butcher in order to keep a shrine. It makes the word knight mean a promise instead of a costume. Watch the complete film. Let the chessboard sit in your mind after the siege is over. Remember that you can be moved by fathers and kings and armies and still have to move yourself. Remember that virtue, when it is inconvenient, is the only hour in which it is actually tested. Remember that Jerusalem, in this telling, is nothing and everything, and that the difference between those two words is whether you can tell a holy stone from a living person. That is the education hidden inside the dust and the flags. That is why the picture survived its first mutilation and became, for those who found the real cut, not a summer casualty but a standard. A cultural icon does not need to win the first weekend. It needs to keep telling the truth after the weekend is forgotten. This one does. It tells you that a kingdom of heaven, if it is anything at all, is not a skyline of captured domes. It is a conscience that will not be rented out, even to a holy war, even to a dying crown, even to the beautiful lie that the city is worth more than the people who will have to bleed for it.

text:
What is "Shield of the Americas"?
"Shield of the Americas" is a coalition of right-wing leaders convened by Trump in Miami in March 2026. Participants included Argentina’s Milei, El Salvador’s Bukele, Ecuador’s Noboa, and Paraguay’s Peña; Kast attended as President-elect. *El País* described the coalition's core objective as "curbing China's influence in Latin America" ​​while coordinating military cooperation to combat drug cartels and criminal organizations. In his opening address, Trump characterized the initiative as a commitment to "using lethal military force to destroy evil cartels and terrorist networks." Kristi Noem was appointed as the coalition's special envoy. The Bachelet Affair: A Second Point of Criticism
Two opposition leaders also took aim at another decision by the Kast administration: the withdrawal of support for former Chilean President Michelle Bachelet’s bid for the UN Secretary-Generalship. Ortiz described the decision as a "mistake," a sign of a "petty attitude," and "very unwise," noting that Chile might have thereby lost the chance to see a Chilean woman lead the UN Secretariat for the first time. Meanwhile, Soto stated that he "still expects Kast to offer a clearer self-critique," though he acknowledged that there were multiple reasons behind Bachelet’s withdrawal from the race.

At a press conference, Kast responded by stating that his government "would not support Bachelet, nor any other candidate," citing disagreements between Chile and Bachelet regarding "how to approach UN governance." However, he also expressed "the utmost respect for Bachelet as an individual and a former president" and hoped to meet with her in the future.

Kast’s Defense
Kast’s own defense of the "Shield of the Americas" initiative centered on the concept of sovereignty. Speaking to reporters in New York, he said, "We have always maintained that every country has its own legislation and its own sovereignty. This does not infringe upon national sovereignty; rather, it aims for horizontal coordination among nations to tackle a new scourge for which many countries are not yet prepared." He drew parallels between this meeting and the Chilean-led "Santiago Agreement," stating that they share the same direction: combating drug trafficking, organized crime, and narco-terrorism. He confirmed he would attend the reception dinner hosted by Trump for national delegations, as well as the "Shield of the Americas" meeting itself.

It is worth noting that Chile has not yet formally joined the "Shield of the Americas" and currently participates in some meetings only as an observer. Kast’s attendance thus carries the nature of an "assessment," though the opposition argues that the President’s personal presence constitutes a de facto endorsement.

The Networks Behind Puntland’s Piracy Resurgence

The resurgence of piracy off Puntland is increasingly revealing a threat that extends well beyond the armed men who board commercial vessels. A new international analysis argues that the networks sustaining piracy now include financiers, weapons suppliers, logistics providers and cross-border connections operating across the Gulf of Aden.

Writing for Responsible Statecraft, Egyptian journalist Khaled Mahmoud Ramadan examines how the widening Iran war and instability across the Greater Red Sea have created openings for piracy to return to waters off Puntland. At least 15 vessels have been attacked in the region this year, compared with five last year, according to International Maritime Organization data cited in the analysis.
The report argues that the renewed piracy problem cannot be understood simply as a failure to patrol Puntland’s coastline. International naval forces have faced competing demands around the Strait of Hormuz, Bab al-Mandab and the Red Sea, while pirate groups have expanded operations farther into the Gulf of Aden and Indian Ocean.
For Puntland, the timing is particularly difficult. Security forces have simultaneously been engaged in the campaign against ISIS in the Cal Miskaad mountains, creating pressure on the forces and resources available for maritime security.
Col. Mohamed Jama, a Puntland maritime-security specialist interviewed by Responsible Statecraft, describes the emerging threat as a cross-border regional network rather than a collection of isolated pirate groups. He says those benefiting from the resurgence include financiers, arms and ammunition suppliers, fuel and logistics providers, khat and drug suppliers, and maritime-smuggling networks. Somali and Yemeni networks, he says, are also moving people, resources and information across the Gulf of Aden.

That distinction matters.

The visible part of piracy takes place at sea. Its infrastructure is largely built on land.

Boats require fuel. Armed groups require weapons, communications and provisions. Hijacked vessels require information about shipping movements. Hostages require places to be held and supplied. Ransoms require negotiators and financial networks capable of moving and distributing money.

Targeting only the men who board vessels therefore leaves much of the system that makes piracy possible intact.

The recent release of MV Sward illustrates the scale of that problem. Responsible Statecraft reports, citing a Puntland maritime source, that approximately $1.7 million in ransom was paid for the vessel and its crew after more than four months in captivity. The ransom figure has not been independently verified.
Sward was seized near Puntland in April. According to the report, pirates subsequently returned to a method familiar from the previous piracy era, using a captured commercial vessel as a mothership from which they could operate farther offshore and support additional attacks.

The financial implications are significant. Every successful multimillion-dollar ransom potentially provides capital that can be reinvested into additional boats, weapons, communications equipment and recruitment. It can also reward the shore-based networks that provide the logistical infrastructure behind operations at sea.

The disputed release of MV LUTUF has raised similar concerns. Puntland rejected Mogadishu’s claim that Somali and Turkish forces militarily liberated the vessel and said instead that it possesses evidence of communications between federal officials and the pirates relating to ransom negotiations. Responsible Statecraft highlights the dispute while noting the wider questions surrounding the operation.

The international dimension is also becoming harder to ignore.

Maritime-security expert Ian Ralby told Responsible Statecraft that the Houthis may be transferring knowledge and technology to Somali pirate networks, potentially increasing their ability to operate across a much wider maritime area. He also said other actors could indirectly benefit from continuing disruption of international shipping. These are analytical assessments rather than established evidence of Houthi direction of individual pirate operations.

What is clearer is that pirate activity has expanded into waters closer to Yemen.

That changes the geography of the threat. Puntland’s piracy problem now sits inside the same maritime system connecting the western Indian Ocean, Gulf of Aden, Bab al-Mandab and Red Sea. Conflict around Hormuz and the Red Sea can therefore create security gaps hundreds of kilometers away along Puntland’s coastline.

Somalia’s State Minister for Foreign Affairs, Ali Omar, offers a different explanation in the Responsible Statecraft analysis. He argues that fragmented security arrangements and parallel security structures create intelligence and accountability gaps, and calls for greater coordination through federal institutions.
But Puntland possesses the security institutions operating on much of the coastline where the current piracy networks are based. Its forces also carry the immediate burden of confronting pirates onshore while simultaneously fighting ISIS in the mountains.

The practical challenge for Puntland is therefore not whether maritime security requires international cooperation. It does. The more consequential question is whether that cooperation strengthens the institutions capable of detecting and dismantling the networks operating from Puntland’s territory.

The emerging threat requires more than patrol boats.

Puntland’s response will increasingly depend on financial intelligence, coastal surveillance, communications interception, criminal investigation and intelligence cooperation capable of identifying the people financing operations, supplying weapons and fuel, negotiating ransoms and moving money after ships are released.

Ports, coastal communities and transportation routes also become part of the security picture. If pirate groups can return from months at sea, transfer ransom proceeds and reconnect with logistics networks ashore, interdiction at sea alone will only disrupt individual operations rather than dismantle the system.

The lesson from Puntland’s previous experience with piracy remains relevant. Piracy becomes substantially harder to suppress once ransom money creates an economic network with enough participants onshore who benefit from its survival.

The current resurgence is therefore a race against consolidation.
Puntland still has functioning security institutions, local knowledge and international partners that were largely absent during the earliest stages of the previous piracy crisis. Those advantages provide an opportunity to attack the networks before they become deeply embedded.

But the focus must move beyond the skiffs visible at sea.

The center of gravity of Puntland’s piracy problem may increasingly lie onshore, among the financiers, suppliers, facilitators and cross-Gulf networks that make every hijacking possible.

text:
STARVIN FOR MARVIN?  MAKE THE CALL SPYTEK!

If Al Davis was still with us, he would’ve already offered a handful of picks to Arizona for Marvin Harrison Jr.

While Harrison’s talent and pedigree is undeniable, something is clearly broken with the Cardinals wide receiver.

Through two weeks of this NFL season, he has been targeted just four times, making one catch for 33 yards.

This is certainly not what the Cardinals expected when they drafted Harrison with the fourth overall pick just two years ago.

Of course nothing is guaranteed when it comes to the draft, every @Raiders  fan knows that, but Harrison was about as sure of a thing as there ever was when he left Ohio State for the NFL.

One scout said, “he’s similar to CeeDee Lamb but stronger, more power and faster.”

Harrison was coming off two amazing college seasons where he made 144 catches for 2474 yards and 28 touchdowns.

His NFL story has not come close to meeting the hype, but I’m hopeful it is still just starting.

Maybe it’s just a change of scenery he needs -- trading one desert for another.

If the price is right, this could be the time for John Spytek to buy that lottery ticket.

I'm certainly not suggesting we need to overpay, but we should definitely find out what it would take.

HOMOLAB tests found the 1TB and 2TB versions use QLC NAND, while 256GB/512GB models use faster TLC storage.

• Worst-case speeds reportedly hit 1.1 MB/s at 60% capacity
• 256GB/512GB models offer faster storage
• Heavy 4K/ProRes video users could notice the slowdown

But paying more for 1TB/2TB and getting slower storage is certainly something power users should know about. 📱💾

text:
This should be a massive wake-up call for the Government.

Almost 7 in 10 young adults are considering leaving Ireland for a better quality of life. And can you really blame them?

People cannot afford to buy a home, rents are through the roof and thousands are caught in the middle — earning too much to qualify for social housing but nowhere near enough to afford a home of their own.

We constantly hear that Ireland is a rich country and that the economy is doing brilliantly. But what does that mean to someone who works every week and still cannot afford somewhere secure to live?

If we keep losing young, skilled and educated people, there will be consequences. Who is going to build our homes, staff our hospitals, run our businesses and pay the taxes that fund public services 10 or 20 years from now?

Then add the cost of food, fuel, electricity and heating as winter approaches.

A rich country should be a country where ordinary working people can afford to live and build a future.

Right now, far too many young people clearly don't believe Ireland offers them that future.

text:
The game doesn't really have to be designed "around" player expression, I'm not saying TN stood around NG1 during development and specificslly used that term while working. 

But regardless the effect of its combat, so many weapons, environment interactivity, enemy interactivity, the amount of moves, all of it created a high skill ceiling and a large amount of player expression. Hence why these games are decades old and still have style communities finding new tech and routes. 

The two greatest CAG's both offer extreme player expression. One of the best if not arguably THE best RPG combat systems (Monster Hunter) offers a ton of player expression and enemy interactivity. This is not a coincidence regardless of if they specifically went out of their way during development to focus on that aspect, it's a natural product of deep combat. 

Difficulty is an outside element from core combat systems, it plays a role yes but just like "more moves doesn't always = better combat" difficulty ≠ better combat either. Dark Souls 1 doesn't have more complex or better designed combat than MGR despite being far harder. 

A game with a very limited moveset can be good, even great. It can even be better than a game that offers more moves. But if you take the exact same game and add more moves, assuming they're well designed and offer more freedom, options and expression, that is an objective improvement.

1/8
A quick fact-check on the recent video from Vara Dark (@DarkTitanMedia) claiming Double Fine is "dunked on," "begging for cash," and ruined by casting Erika Ishii.
When you strip away the culture-war outrage farming, the narrative falls apart under basic industry reality. 🧵👇
2/8
Claim 1: Double Fine is "begging for cash" and failing.
Double Fine literally pioneered modern video game crowdfunding with Broken Age ($3.3M in 2012).
Raising $550,000+ from 6,600+ backers isn't "desperation"—it’s an independent studio rallying its core community after negotiating an exit from Xbox to keep their IP and creative autonomy intact.
3/8
Claim 2: The $100M Brütal Legend 2 stretch goal shows delusion.
Taking a $100 million stretch goal literally shows zero familiarity with Double Fine.
Tim Schafer has built 20+ years of studio culture on self-aware, deadpan satire. A ridiculous $100M goal for a sequel requiring massive music licensing is an obvious running gag for fans, not an earnest budget projection.
4/8
Claim 3: Erika Ishii is an "untalented liability."
Dismissing Ishii ignores a massive, proven resume: Ghost of Yōtei (Atsu), Apex Legends (Valkyrie), Destiny 2, Cyberpunk 2077, Dragon Age, and Dropout/Dimension 20.
More importantly: Double Fine confirmed Ishii offered their talent pro bono to support an indie studio's independence. That's solidarity, not a cash grab.
5/8
Claim 4: Locking replies proves Double Fine "can't take criticism."
The announcement thread wasn't flooded with thoughtful game design critiques; it was hit with coordinated brigading, bad-faith spam, and personal attacks targeting Ishii.
Locking a thread to shield your team and collaborators from harassment is basic community duty of care, not fragility.
6/8
Claim 5: Consulting with Anita Sarkeesian "ruined" Psychonauts 2.
Revisionist history at its finest. Psychonauts 2 launched to universal acclaim (87–89 Metascore) and multiple Game of the Year nominations.
Studios hire narrative consultants all the time to handle delicate themes like mental health and neurodivergence. It sharpened the writing; it didn’t sanitize it.
7/8
Claim 6: "Woke DEI" caused Double Fine’s challenges.
Double Fine’s recent restructuring mirrors brutal layoffs across Microsoft, Sony, and the broader tech sector due to post-pandemic corrections and production costs.
Double Fine’s hallmark has always been quirky, empathetic storytelling (Grim Fandango, Psychonauts). Blaming macroeconomics on "wokeness" is lazy rage-bait.
8/8
Manufacturing outrage requires turning studio independence into "begging," a running gag into "delusion," and pro bono collaboration into a conspiracy.
Double Fine survived publisher consolidation, kept their IP, and funded their next game in days. That's an indie win.
For reference, you can review the original critique and framing discussed here in Vara Dark's commentary on Erika Ishii and Double Fine. This video is relevant as it provides the primary talking points and commentary regarding Double Fine's crowdfunding campaign and casting decisions addressed in this breakdown.

text:
Yellow line doesn’t indicate the full picture.  Employees can invest those wages and avail themselves of tools to take advantage of this huge corporate growth surge. And many have,  for example here’s what’s available to an average worker: 

•Buy stocks / index funds / ETFs directly (brokerage, IRA, Roth IRA). No employer required. This is how most people actually ride the corporate-earnings surge.
•401(k) / 403(b) invested in stock funds. Same idea, tax-advantaged, often with an employer match.
•ESPP — buy employer stock at a discount (usually 10–15%). Offered by ~57% of public companies. Median participation ~38%.
•RSUs / stock options — company grants stock or the right to buy it. Common for salaried staff at public/tech firms; rare for many hourly jobs.
•ESOP — company-funded retirement trust that holds employer stock. ~11 million active participants, ~$2 trillion in assets.
Who owns the growth
•~62% of U.S. adults own stock (including funds and retirement accounts).
•~58% of households held stocks as of the 2022 Fed SCF.
•Top 10% of households own ~87% of household stock wealth.
•Gallup: 87% of $100k+ households own stock vs. 28% of households under $50k.

The actual wealth these tools have created (documented counts) is staggering: 
•Fidelity 401(k)s: 769,000 accounts ≥ $1 million (Q2 2026); ~3% of its 25.8 million 401(k)s. Average 401(k) balance $155,800; median $35,800. Typical millionaire: age ~58, ~25 years of saving. IRA millionaires on the same platform: 684,140.
•SpaceX IPO (2026): ~4,400 employee millionaires; ~400 above $100 million.
•AutoZone: 4,000+ lower-level employee millionaires via discounts/options/401(k) stock.
•Microsoft: historically cited as ~12,000 rank-and-file millionaires by the mid-2000s from options (later estimates higher; not an official census).
•Tesla: Musk has said production-line workers became millionaires; 44 U.S. employees received $1M+ grants in 2020–21. No full public millionaire count.
•ESOPs: studied S-corp ESOP balances roughly double comparable 401(k)s; younger employee-owners show much higher household wealth than peers without ownership.
Fact that matches the chart: wages grew ~30% since 1990; corporate earnings ~1,300%. Anyone who owned a broad stock index captured most of that earnings/market boom. Anyone limited to wages, or who never enrolled in an ESPP/401(k)/brokerage, did not.

Like companies employees can and should invest to grow their wealth - base salary is there to provide day-to-day needs etc. but the future is built by investing.

00–04 — Indonesian railway platform:
She stands too close to the safe platform edge while looking down the line. Indonesian commuter train approaches. Boyfriend's hand gently pulls her backward behind the tactile strip in one continuous movement. Train passes safely; wind moves her scarf and cardigan. She looks startled, then relieved.

04–06 — Yogyakarta tropical path:
She walks hand-in-hand with boyfriend through lush greenery, turns back and laughs.

06–08 — Yogyakarta batik shop:
She discovers colorful batik fabrics, touches one and smiles at the camera.

08–09 — Local Yogyakarta street:
She crosses an ordinary street in her long Indonesian outfit, then looks back playfully.

09–11 — Traditional Yogyakarta lane:
Tiled-roof houses, scooters, small warungs and tropical plants. She walks ahead and turns back smiling.

11–13 — Prambanan, Central Java:
Green surroundings with authentic Prambanan temple architecture in the distance. She points toward it, then looks at boyfriend.

13–14 — Indonesian dessert stall:
She tastes a traditional iced dessert and playfully offers a spoonful toward the camera.

14–16 — Small Indonesian warung:
Vegetarian noodles with vegetables, tofu and mushrooms. Focus pulls from steaming food to her smiling face.

16–17 — Local bookshop:
She browses an illustrated book and smiles curiously.

17–19 — Central Java greenery:
A calm local animal approaches while she laughs from a safe distance.

19–20 — Quiet reading:
She reads beneath a tropical tree; close details of her hands, tunik embroidery and scarf.

20–23 — Kali Code, Yogyakarta:
She walks beside the river, stops at a safe railing, turns back and reaches her hand toward the boyfriend.

23–25 — Yogyakarta rice fields:
Golden-hour green rice fields. She walks slowly, turns toward camera and gives a soft genuine smile.

25–27 — Yogyakarta night market:
Warm Indonesian lights and food stalls. She jogs a few steps ahead, turns back laughing and waits for boyfriend.

27–28 — Scarf detail:
Close handheld shot of her adjusting her cream Indonesian scarf and batik brooch beside her woven bag.

28–30 — Final laughter:
Warm night-market lights behind her. She notices the camera, laughs, reaches toward the lens and smiles directly at boyfriend. Natural camera shake. End exactly at 30 seconds.

News Flashback

Jan-March 2026

Streaming Wars

The "Streaming Wars" refers to the intense competition among digital media platforms to dominate the subscription video-on-demand (SVOD) market by capturing and retaining global audiences.

As of early 2026, the landscape has shifted from a period of rapid expansion into a phase of major consolidation and a focus on profitability over subscriber volume.

The "Winner" and Current State (2026)

Netflix Dominance: Industry analysts increasingly cite Netflix as the victor. In January 2026, Netflix reported 18% year-over-year revenue growth and is currently pursuing a high-stakes $83 billion all-cash acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery’s studio and streaming assets (including HBO/Max).

The "Big 3": Despite fierce competition, the market is primarily dominated by Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, and Disney+.

YouTube's Rise: Some experts argue YouTube is the true winner of the broader attention economy, surpassing traditional streaming services in total viewership by pivoting back to user-generated content.

Key Strategies in 2026

Consolidation: Smaller or struggling services are being shuttered or merged. For example, Disney recently shut down Hulu as a standalone service.

Monetization Shifts: Platforms have moved away from "growth at all costs" to strategies like password-sharing crackdowns, ad-supported tiers, and price hikes.

Live Sports & Events: Services are increasingly bidding on live sports rights (e.g., Netflix hosting WWE's Raw starting in 2025) to differentiate their offerings.

Bundling: To combat "subscription fatigue," platforms are forming strategic partnerships with telecommunications companies and banks to offer bundled service hubs.

Consumer Impact

Price Hikes: Many consumers are canceling services due to rising costs; over 40% of Americans cited price as their primary reason for unsubscribing in late 2025.

Resurgence of Piracy: Fragmented content and high costs have led to a significant comeback for pirate sites, which some users now find more comprehensive than paid services.

"South Park: The Streaming Wars": The term was popularized in mainstream culture by a 2-part South Park special released on Paramount+ in 2022, which satirized the industry's aggressive competition.

Gold (1974)

Gold is a 1974 British action-thriller directed by Peter R. Hunt, starring Roger Moore and Susannah York. Based on the 1970 novel Gold Mine by Wilbur Smith, the film is set in the South African goldfields and follows a conspiracy by a global syndicate to manipulate the price of gold by sabotaging a rich mine.

Plot: Rod Slater (Moore), a newly appointed general manager, is manipulated by his boss, Manfred Steyner (Bradford Dillman), into drilling through a protective barrier into a subterranean lake. This is intended to flood the mine, causing a global gold shortage and driving up prices for a greedy cabal.

Production Controversy: The film was controversially shot on location in South Africa during the apartheid era. This led to a "black ban" by British film unions, though some crew members defied it to work on the production.

James Bond Connection: Many crew members were veterans of the James Bond franchise, including director Peter Hunt (On Her Majesty's Secret Service), editor John Glen, and title designer Maurice Binder.

Accolades: The film received an Academy Award nomination for Best Original Song for "Wherever Love Takes Me," composed by Elmer Bernstein and sung by Maureen McGovern.

Streaming Wars

The "Streaming Wars" refers to the intense competition among digital media platforms to dominate the subscription video-on-demand (SVOD) market by capturing and retaining global audiences.

As of early 2026, the landscape has shifted from a period of rapid expansion into a phase of major consolidation and a focus on profitability over subscriber volume.

The "Winner" and Current State (2026)

Netflix Dominance: Industry analysts increasingly cite Netflix as the victor. In January 2026, Netflix reported 18% year-over-year revenue growth and is currently pursuing a high-stakes $83 billion all-cash acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery’s studio and streaming assets (including HBO/Max).

The "Big 3": Despite fierce competition, the market is primarily dominated by Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, and Disney+.

YouTube's Rise: Some experts argue YouTube is the true winner of the broader attention economy, surpassing traditional streaming services in total viewership by pivoting back to user-generated content.

Key Strategies in 2026

Consolidation: Smaller or struggling services are being shuttered or merged. For example, Disney recently shut down Hulu as a standalone service.

Monetization Shifts: Platforms have moved away from "growth at all costs" to strategies like password-sharing crackdowns, ad-supported tiers, and price hikes.

Live Sports & Events: Services are increasingly bidding on live sports rights (e.g., Netflix hosting WWE's Raw starting in 2025) to differentiate their offerings.

Bundling: To combat "subscription fatigue," platforms are forming strategic partnerships with telecommunications companies and banks to offer bundled service hubs.

Consumer Impact

Price Hikes: Many consumers are canceling services due to rising costs; over 40% of Americans cited price as their primary reason for unsubscribing in late 2025.

Resurgence of Piracy: Fragmented content and high costs have led to a significant comeback for pirate sites, which some users now find more comprehensive than paid services.

"South Park: The Streaming Wars": The term was popularized in mainstream culture by a 2-part South Park special released on Paramount+ in 2022, which satirized the industry's aggressive competition.

BASKETball courts
One of the most famous parquet floors is that used by the Boston Celtics of the @NBA . The original floor, which was installed at the Celtics' original home of Boston Arena in 1946, was moved intact to Boston Garden in 1952 and used there until the team moved to what was then known as FleetCenter in 1995, now known as TD Garden. The floor remained intact and in use until it was cut up and sold as souvenirs in 1999, after the 1998 demolition of Boston Garden. The Celtics today play on a parquet floor inside TD Garden that combines old and new sections. In 2018, the Celtics constructed a new parquet floor for use in their new Auerbach Center practice facility. It is the only NBA court floor made from red oak; all others are made from rock maple.[2] In 2023, the Celtics played on a traditional maple court at home for the first time during the 2023 NBA in-season tournament.[3] The Celtics petitioned the NBA to include the parquet pattern on its in-season tournament court, but were denied.[4] In the 2024 NBA Cup, however, the Celtics' parquet pattern was included on their tournament court design.[5]

Similar square-paneled parquet floors, albeit in maple, were made for the Orlando Magic, Minnesota Timberwolves, Denver Nuggets, and New Jersey Nets. Of the four, only the Magic continue to use a square-paneled parquet floor, which was first used at the Orlando Arena in 1989 and later moved to Amway Center (now Kia Center) in 2010. The Nets debuted their parquet at the Meadowlands Arena in 1988, and continued to use the floor until 1997; the floor remained in use with the Seton Hall basketball team until 2007. The Nuggets used a parquet floor from 1990 to 1993 at the McNichols Sports Arena, while the Timberwolves played on a parquet floor from 1996 to 2008 at the Target Center. The Timberwolves brought back the parquet floor for select games in the 2025–26 season while wearing the black throwback uniforms.

In 1995, the Toronto Raptors debuted with a herringbone parquet, and used the floor until 1999 while playing in three different home venues: SkyDome (now Rogers Centre), Copps Coliseum (now TD Coliseum) and Maple Leaf Gardens. The now-Brooklyn Nets introduced chevron parquet flooring upon moving to the Barclays Center in 2012. However, its sister WNBA team (since 2019), the New York Liberty, continues to use a traditional floor at the venue. In 2025, the Golden State Valkyries debuted a vertical herringbone floor at Chase Center; its NBA counterpart, the Golden State Warriors, still uses a traditional court.

While the Charlotte Hornets unveiled a parquet-like floor at the Time Warner Cable Arena for the 2014–15 season, it is not considered a true parquet floor. Instead, it simulated the pattern of the parquet by alternately painting light and dark trapezoid sections through the use of varnish, forming a beehive pattern that is synonymous with the franchise. In 2021, the Hornets changed its court design, relegating the trapezoids to midcourt.

News Flashback

Jan-March 2026

Streaming Wars

The "Streaming Wars" refers to the intense competition among digital media platforms to dominate the subscription video-on-demand (SVOD) market by capturing and retaining global audiences.

As of early 2026, the landscape has shifted from a period of rapid expansion into a phase of major consolidation and a focus on profitability over subscriber volume.

The "Winner" and Current State (2026)

Netflix Dominance: Industry analysts increasingly cite Netflix as the victor. In January 2026, Netflix reported 18% year-over-year revenue growth and is currently pursuing a high-stakes $83 billion all-cash acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery’s studio and streaming assets (including HBO/Max).

The "Big 3": Despite fierce competition, the market is primarily dominated by Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, and Disney+.

YouTube's Rise: Some experts argue YouTube is the true winner of the broader attention economy, surpassing traditional streaming services in total viewership by pivoting back to user-generated content.

Key Strategies in 2026

Consolidation: Smaller or struggling services are being shuttered or merged. For example, Disney recently shut down Hulu as a standalone service.

Monetization Shifts: Platforms have moved away from "growth at all costs" to strategies like password-sharing crackdowns, ad-supported tiers, and price hikes.

Live Sports & Events: Services are increasingly bidding on live sports rights (e.g., Netflix hosting WWE's Raw starting in 2025) to differentiate their offerings.

Bundling: To combat "subscription fatigue," platforms are forming strategic partnerships with telecommunications companies and banks to offer bundled service hubs.

Consumer Impact

Price Hikes: Many consumers are canceling services due to rising costs; over 40% of Americans cited price as their primary reason for unsubscribing in late 2025.

Resurgence of Piracy: Fragmented content and high costs have led to a significant comeback for pirate sites, which some users now find more comprehensive than paid services.

"South Park: The Streaming Wars": The term was popularized in mainstream culture by a 2-part South Park special released on Paramount+ in 2022, which satirized the industry's aggressive competition.

Gold (1974)

Gold is a 1974 British action-thriller directed by Peter R. Hunt, starring Roger Moore and Susannah York. Based on the 1970 novel Gold Mine by Wilbur Smith, the film is set in the South African goldfields and follows a conspiracy by a global syndicate to manipulate the price of gold by sabotaging a rich mine.

Plot: Rod Slater (Moore), a newly appointed general manager, is manipulated by his boss, Manfred Steyner (Bradford Dillman), into drilling through a protective barrier into a subterranean lake. This is intended to flood the mine, causing a global gold shortage and driving up prices for a greedy cabal.

Production Controversy: The film was controversially shot on location in South Africa during the apartheid era. This led to a "black ban" by British film unions, though some crew members defied it to work on the production.

James Bond Connection: Many crew members were veterans of the James Bond franchise, including director Peter Hunt (On Her Majesty's Secret Service), editor John Glen, and title designer Maurice Binder.

Accolades: The film received an Academy Award nomination for Best Original Song for "Wherever Love Takes Me," composed by Elmer Bernstein and sung by Maureen McGovern.

text:
On 22 September 1735, NUMBER 10 GETS ITS FIRST PRIME MINISTER: Sir Robert Walpole moved into the house we now know as 10 Downing Street, becoming the first British prime minister to live there. Though, strictly speaking, neither “prime minister” nor “Number 10” was yet quite official.

Walpole had served as First Lord of the Treasury since 1721 and is generally regarded as Britain’s first prime minister because he performed the role before the title was formally established.

King George II had offered him the Downing Street property as a personal gift in 1732. Walpole declined to accept it for himself. Instead, he asked that it be assigned to the office of First Lord of the Treasury, making it an official residence for him and his successors. It was a remarkably important decision. A private royal gift became a residence attached to public office; a tradition that continues nearly three centuries later.

The house Walpole entered was not quite the Number 10 familiar today. Architect William Kent had spent approximately three years joining the Downing Street townhouse to a larger building overlooking Horse Guards and refurbishing the resulting residence.

It wasn't even numbered 10 yet. The house was originally numbered 5 and acquired its famous address when Downing Street was renumbered in 1779. The present black door and many of its familiar fittings also came later.

Behind the modest frontage was a substantial residence of dozens of rooms. Walpole used a large ground-floor room as his study; it later became the Cabinet Room, where governments still meet.

The day after moving in, Walpole held his first formal reception there. Within days, Queen Caroline and other members of the Royal Family had called for breakfast; an admirably British beginning for one of the world’s most recognisable political addresses.

Not every subsequent prime minister chose to live there. Many preferred their own, grander London houses, while Number 10 developed an unfortunate reputation for cracked walls, sinking floors and troublesome foundations. Nevertheless, the convention Walpole established endured.

The famous brass letterbox still bears the words:
FIRST LORD OF THE TREASURY

So, on this day in 1735, Britain’s first prime minister crossed the threshold of a house that was not yet Number 10 and quietly began a tradition at the heart of British government.

text:
The Greenland agreement is a win for all three countries. The only people who need it to be a humiliation are the ones addicted to spite politics and zero-sum ideology.

Denmark is not some freeloading extra in this story. It is a NATO founding member. It brought Greenland into the alliance. After the Cold War it rebuilt for actual wars and showed up: Kosovo, Afghanistan, Iraq. It backed Iraq war when France and Germany walked out. In Helmand it took high-risk missions with few caveats. About 50 Danish soldiers were killed. Per capita, that is in the same brutal neighborhood as American losses.

It has hosted United States at Pituffik, the old Thule base, under the 1951 defense agreement for decades. That site is crucial for missile warning, missile defense, space surveillance. No other European ally offers an equivalent Arctic and North Atlantic platform.

Greenland is not being “taken.” It is being written into the deal as a party. That matters. Greenlanders accept the United States as a strategic partner and ally. They will not accept it as an owner. Fine. The United States already gets what it actually needs in the Arctic: access, overflight, more basing, and a lock against Chinese or Russian bases and sensitive investment. Sovereignty stays with the Kingdom. Self-determination stays with Greenlanders. Security becomes trilateral and, as Copenhagen is saying, NATO-shaped rather than a bilateral shouting match.

Stop asking who lost. This is one of the rare agreements that gives Washington the Arctic depth it wants, gives Denmark an end to a crisis that never should have been turned into a loyalty test, and gives Greenland a partner without a transfer of title.

Credit both sides. Trump forced the issue until the security architecture was updated for a world with Russia and China in the High North. Mette Frederiksen kept an ally from becoming an adversary and still brought home recognition of Danish sovereignty. That is statecraft, not surrender. Stop antagonizing a country that has already bled with you. Take the win and move on.

Trita Parsi offers an interesting explanation for one of the strangest dynamics of the Iran war: Riyadh wants American help against the Houthis, but remains deeply reluctant to give Washington the military access it could use against Iran. 

That reluctance has already had consequences. Earlier in the war, Saudi Arabia refused to allow the United States to use its bases and airspace for Project Freedom, the planned U.S. operation to escort commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

The operation was subsequently shelved. Now the equation has changed.

The Houthis have expanded their campaign against Saudi Arabia, while Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has asked Washington for military assistance against them.

Parsi argues that some in the Trump administration see an opportunity for a bargain: U.S. help against the Houthis in exchange for renewed Saudi access for American operations.

From Riyadh's perspective, however, the trade is potentially dangerous.

“You’re essentially trading a war with the Houthis for a direct war with Iran.”

That gets to the heart of the Saudi dilemma.

Riyadh wants U.S. military power when confronting the Houthi threat on its southern flank. What it does not necessarily want is for Saudi territory to become the launchpad for a renewed American campaign against Iran, potentially making the kingdom itself a direct Iranian target.

text:
If you are curious why Ireland so consistently lines up with the Palestinians against the State of Israel, the short version that gets repeated in Dublin, Belfast nationalist areas, and Irish political speeches is a story of two small peoples who suffered British rule, partition, displacement, and a long fight to be recognised as a nation. That story is real enough as a feeling. It is also incomplete, and the missing pieces sit in the same decade and the same logic that later got dressed up as standing with the oppressed and with minorities.

Irish republicanism learned early that Britain’s difficulty could be Ireland’s opportunity. In the late 1930s the IRA, then a small but determined organisation whose goal was a united Ireland free of British control, opened channels to Nazi Germany. Seán Russell, IRA chief of staff, wrote to the German ambassador offering help in any future war with Britain. James O’Donovan travelled to Hamburg to discuss arms, money, and sabotage. German agents landed in Ireland. One of them, Hermann Görtz, parachuted in to work with the IRA on what became known as Plan Kathleen: a German landing in the north supported by an IRA rising that would seize key points and help throw the British out of Northern Ireland. In 1940 Russell and Frank Ryan boarded a German U boat bound for Ireland on a mission called Operation Dove; Russell died at sea and the landing never happened. IRA statements that summer called the Germans friends and liberators of the Irish people and predicted that, with their victorious European allies, Ireland would soon have absolute independence. The Irish government interned many of these men and the plans were amateurish and failed. That does not erase the fact that the armed republican movement, the same political tradition that later produced Sinn Féin and the murals that still say one struggle, treated Hitler’s Germany as a usable partner because Germany was at war with Britain.

Official Ireland was neutral. Éamon de Valera’s government interned the IRA, secretly passed some information that helped the Allies, and sent tens of thousands of Irish volunteers into British uniform. Neutrality was also performed with a rigidity that produced one of the most remembered diplomatic gestures of the war: on 2 May 1945 de Valera personally called on the German minister in Dublin to offer condolences on Hitler’s death. He later insisted it was only courtesy to a diplomat and consistency with the same protocol he had used when Roosevelt died. The rest of the world, watching the camps being opened, saw something else. A large part of Irish nationalist opinion had spent the war years treating Germany as the lesser problem and Britain as the permanent one. That is not the same as a nation of Nazi enthusiasts. It is the same reflex that later made it easy to treat Israel as the new Britain and the Palestinians as the new Irish.

The Palestinian national movement of the same years ran on a parallel track. Haj Amin al Husseini, Grand Mufti of Jerusalem and the dominant figure in Palestinian Arab politics under the British Mandate, fled first to Iraq and then to Berlin. He met Hitler in November 1941, lived in a villa taken from a Jewish family, broadcast Nazi propaganda to the Arab world, recruited Bosnian Muslims into the Waffen SS Handschar division, and worked to stop Jews from leaving Europe for Palestine even when that meant they would be sent to camps instead. He wanted the same things the IRA wanted from Germany: an ally against Britain and the destruction of a Jewish national project that the British had, however reluctantly, begun to tolerate. After the war he was not discarded by the Palestinian national movement; he remained a reference point. The later PLO and the armed groups that trained or talked with the Provisional IRA in the 1970s inherited that lineage even if they wrapped it in leftist language.

When Irish republicans and Irish public opinion later looked at Israel and Palestine they did not start from a blank sheet of human rights. They started from a template already written: the British partitioned us, the British partitioned them, the settlers and the army and the wall look like the Black and Tans and internment and the border. Zionists had once been fellow anti British rebels; once they accepted partition and built a state that won wars, they became the occupier in the Irish story. Sinn Féin and the IRA cultivated the PLO as a sister movement. Murals in Belfast put IRA and PLO fighters under the same slogan. That alliance was never mainly about Jews as a minority or about liberal democracy. It was about two nationalist movements that had already shown they would take help from whoever was fighting their particular empire.

The claim that this is simply solidarity with the oppressed and with minorities therefore has to sit next to the record. The IRA of 1940 was ready to help a regime that was murdering Jews, Roma, Slavs, and political enemies on an industrial scale because that regime was useful against Britain. The leading Palestinian Arab politician of the same years did the same, with added religious antisemitism and a direct effort to keep Jews from reaching safety in Palestine. Modern Ireland’s political class and a large share of its public still read the conflict through the older republican lens: Israel is the powerful, partitioned, Western backed state; Palestine is the unfinished national project. That reading produces genuine anger at civilian death in Gaza and genuine support for recognition of a Palestinian state. It also produces a selective memory that treats the Nazi collaborations as footnotes instead of evidence that “the oppressed” in this particular tradition have not always chosen their friends by how those friends treated minorities.

The result is a foreign policy and a street politics that feel morally obvious inside Ireland and look one sided from outside it. Ireland recognised Palestine, pushed the Occupied Territories Bill, and treats the conflict as a domestic political issue in a way few other Western countries do. Polls show far higher sympathy for Palestinians than for Israelis and far higher engagement with the conflict than geography or trade would predict. The colonial parallel and the republican inheritance explain most of that. The earlier willingness of both the IRA and the Mufti’s movement to work with the Nazis explains why the parallel was available in the first place and why the language of standing with the oppressed can be used so confidently even when the historical record of both movements includes deals with the regime that defined modern industrial oppression of minorities. The issues are not separate. They are the same habit of mind applied to a different map.

text:
The Paradox of UN Assembly Power:

Hans Morgenthau looks at why the UN General Assembly's inability to enforce its decisions doesn't destroy it, but actually keeps powerful nations from leaving:

The rain over the East River had turned the glass grey, blurring the tugboats moving slowly towards Queens. Inside the lounge, coffee cups rattled against silver trays as diplomats from newly independent nations argued in small clusters near the window.

A young legal advisor attached to a European delegation set down his notes with a sharp tap of his pencil. "There were 64 votes in favour, six against, and zero legal obligation," he said, shaking his head.

"The Assembly passes resolutions as if they were law, but the great powers simply walk out of the room and ignore them. It makes the entire institution look like an expensive talking shop."

Hans Morgenthau didn't look up from his pipe immediately. He watched a puff of blue smoke rise and dissipate against the low ceiling before turning his grey eyes towards the young lawyer.

"You speak as though the absence of enforcement is a tragic flaw," Morgenthau said softly, his German accent grounding the room. "Have you considered what would happen tomorrow if Assembly resolutions were legally binding?"

"Order would replace anarchy," the lawyer answered without hesitation. "A true international parliament. If 64 nations vote to condemn an aggression or enforce a border, that decision would carry the legitimate force of world law."

"And if those 64 nations vote to compel a superpower to dismantle its primary radar defence network or surrender a vital strategic strait?" Morgenthau asked. "What does that superpower do?"

"It would be legally bound to comply," the lawyer said.

"Legal obligation is a sentence on paper," Morgenthau replied, leaning forward. "Physical survival is a law of nature.

Tell me, if a state possesses 300 atomic warheads, 4 million men under arms, and the physical capacity to flatten its neighbours, will its government allow its national survival to be voted away by 30 small island republics and 20 landlocked territories whose combined military strength couldn't secure a single harbour?"

The lawyer frowned, shifting in his leather chair. "If they refuse to comply, they become an outlaw state."

"And then?" Morgenthau pressed.

"When the outlaw state refuses to dismantle its defence, what happens to your parliament? Either the majority must raise an army to invade the superpower, which means total global war, or the superpower simply leaves the United Nations and tears up the charter."

The room grew quiet around them. Outside, the horn of a river barge sounded twice through the mist.

"If the Assembly possessed real legal power," Morgenthau continued, "great powers would be forced to choose between two unacceptable outcomes: submit their vital security to a numerical headcount of minor states, or destroy the organisation that seeks to coerce them. They'd choose destruction every single time.

A world government with majoritarian voting power can't coexist with extreme physical power asymmetries among its members."

The lawyer tapped his pencil against the table again, slower this time. "So you're saying the Security Council veto exists to protect real power, while the Assembly exists to ignore it."

"The Security Council reflects physical reality," Morgenthau said. "The veto acknowledges that you can't coerce a great power without triggering a world war. Therefore, no action can be taken under law where physical power can't enforce it.

But the Assembly operates on an entirely different mechanism. It offers absolute sovereign equality, one country, one vote, regardless of whether that country is China or Luxembourg."

"Which is why its resolutions are merely recommendations," the lawyer said slowly, the mechanism beginning to take shape in his mind. "If the Assembly had binding power, sovereign equality would become an existential threat to the powerful."

"Precisely," Morgenthau said.

"The nonbinding character of Assembly resolutions isn't a failure of design; it is the exact structural condition that permits great powers to remain in the same room with small ones. It decouples political expression from existential coercion. A superpower can accept being outvoted by 50 small nations on a moral declaration precisely because that declaration can't send a fleet to its shores or strip its sovereign territory."

"It functions as a pressure relief valve," the lawyer murmured.

"It functions as an information market," Morgenthau corrected gently.

"It allows great powers to measure global public sentiment and hear the grievances of small states without risking their vital national interests. It gives small states a global platform to mobilise international opinion without giving them the legal authority to trigger a war they can't fight."

"So if we gave the Assembly the power we always claim to want," the lawyer said, "we'd destroy the UN within a week."

"The day Assembly resolutions become legally enforceable is the day the great powers walk out for the last time," Morgenthau said, placing his pipe back in his pocket.

"The weakness of the vote is what keeps the powerful inside the building."

***
Hans Morgenthau (1904-1980) was a German born US political scientist and leading figure in political realism. His 1948 work Politics Among Nations argued that international relations are driven by states pursuing power and national interest.

The UN General Assembly gives every member country an equal vote, but it can't enforce its decisions.

text:
Look at me. People often call me the parliament of the world.

Inside my large hall in New York, 193 sovereign states sit together. Every country gets one desk, one microphone, and one vote. The smallest island country with 11,000 citizens has the exact same voting power as a country with 1.4 billion people.

In 1945, when 51 founding states wrote my rules, the goal seemed simple. They wanted a place where every country on Earth could talk instead of fight.

But right away, a deep contradiction appears. If I look like a global parliament, why can't I pass actual laws?

When a national parliament votes on a law, police enforce it and citizens must obey. When my members vote on a resolution, nothing automatically changes on the ground. My resolutions aren't legally binding on sovereign countries. A government can vote against my text, ignore it completely, and walk away without breaking my rules.

So what am I actually made of? I don't have an army. I don't collect national taxes. I can't arrest anyone.

If I can't force anyone to obey, why do 193 governments send their diplomats to sit in my hall for months every year? Why do states fight for days over a single word in my documents?

The answer lies in how power works. Raw force can win a fight, but force alone can't make an action seem right to the rest of the world.

Governments need something force can't buy. They need legitimacy.

When a nation acts alone, other states suspect its motives. But when my assembly passes a resolution by a two thirds majority, that vote shows what the world community considers acceptable.

I turn private desires into global standards. A resolution might not send soldiers, but it tells every government, bank, and international court who is acting inside accepted norms and who is breaking them.

That reveals a deeper problem. If I hold global opinion, why do major wars still happen despite my votes?

To understand that, I must look at the rest of the United Nations system. When the system was built in 1945, power was split into two separate parts.

I was given global debate and equal representation. Another smaller room, the Security Council, was given executive power to use force and impose sanctions.

Fifteen states sit in that room, and five permanent powers hold a veto. If one of those five powerful states says no/bù/nyet/non, the Security Council freezes. Hard power lives in a room that is often locked by political disagreement.

So what happens when the Security Council freezes during a major crisis?

In 1950, my members created a special rule called Uniting for Peace. It states that if the Security Council fails to maintain peace because of a veto, I can step in.

I still can't command armies, but I can recommend collective action and isolate an aggressive state.

When the big powers block each other, I become the only place left where the rest of the world can speak with one voice. I can't stop a tank directly, but I can make the diplomatic, legal, and economic cost of using that tank much higher.

Now my true nature becomes clear.

I'm not a world government, because a real government holds a monopoly on force. Nor am I just a talking shop, because talking shops don't set international legal standards, manage multibillion dollar budgets, or welcome new countries onto the world map.

I'm an institutional marketplace for global legitimacy.

Powerful nations bring their strength to my floor because even the strongest country wants its actions to look lawful. Small nations come because my one nation, one vote rule gives them a voice they could never command through military power.

My power stops at the edge of national sovereignty. I can't force a state to help its people or stop a war if its leaders choose to ignore global consensus.

My strength exists only as long as my members choose to value their reputation among other states.

Yet as long as sovereign countries exist and want to avoid total conflict, they must gather somewhere to agree on the rules of the planet.

I'm where physical force comes to seek moral permission, and where the quietest countries stand on equal ground with the most powerful.

***
The United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) is the main deliberative organ of the United Nations, where all 193 member states meet with equal voting power to debate global issues, approve the organisation budget, and pass international resolutions.

🇫🇷 French defence procurement agency, DGA has delivered the first Jaguar R3 armored reconnaissance and combat vehicles to the French Army. @DGA @armeedeTerre 

According to DGA, the delivery commenced this summer, with a total of 21 vehicles delivered by September 4.

The R3 version incorporates all the technical and operational capabilities of the Jaguar and includes the integration of MMP missiles. The DGA and the Army declared the new R3 version combat-ready on April 8, with the Army authorizing the use of this version on July 20.

French Army is expected to take delivery of 238 Jaguar vehicles by 2030, with all 300 vehicles expected to be delivered by 2035. The vehicles will equip seven of the Army's armoured cavalry regiments.

The vehicles already delivered and in service with the forces are undergoing a retrofit campaign to the R3 standard, which will be completed by the end of 2027.

EBRC Jaguar is a six-wheeled armoured fighting vehicle operated by the French Army. It is a component of the French SCORPION programme, which also include the VBMR-L Serval 4x4 light multi-role armored vehicle and the VBMR Griffon 6x6 multi-role armored vehicle.

The vehicle is armed with a 40mm cannon using telescoped ammunition and a remotely operated turret equipped with a 7.62mm machine gun as secondary armament for short-range self-defense. Jaguar is intended to replace the French Army's AMX-10RC and ERC-90 Sagaie vehicles, as well as the VAB armored personnel carriers equipped with HOT anti-tank missiles (VAB HOT).

The vehicle weighs 25 tons and offers a high level of protection against mines and IEDs. It is designed for armoured reconnaissance as well as for combat in complex environments such as urban and mountainous areas.

The Jaguar is developed and manufactured by KNDS France, Arquus and Thales, with the final assembly taking place at the KNDS industrial site in Roanne (42). Safran Group is responsible for the vehicle's optronics, CTA International supplies the 40mm CTAS cannon, and MBDA supplies the MMP missile. @KNDS_France @Arquus_Defense @thalesgroup @SAFRAN @MBDAFrance

text:
A professional baseball team is about to pay more than double a player's remaining salary this year, and none of the extra money is going to the player at all.

+
+
+
+
+

The New York Yankees are set to claim right-hander John Schreiber off waivers from the Kansas City Royals, as reported by Joel Sherman of The New York Post. Schreiber is owed roughly $535,000 for the rest of his $3.715 million salary this season, and under standard waiver procedure, whichever team claims him also takes on that remaining obligation. For most organizations, that would be the end of the arithmetic. Not for the Yankees. As a third-time payor over the top line of Major League Baseball's competitive balance tax, the Yankees are subject to a 110% surcharge on any payroll they add during the season. The result: adding Schreiber will cost the organization roughly $1.1 million in total, more than double the salary itself, with the difference flowing entirely into the league's tax system rather than to the player.

The timing is no accident. Late August is peak season for waiver activity across the league, since a player can be placed on waivers without losing his roster spot, letting a team quietly offer him to the rest of baseball in hopes another club claims him and absorbs the contract. September 1 sharpens the incentive further, since it is the deadline for a player to be on a roster in order to be playoff-eligible, making claims far more likely right before that date than after. Active rosters also expand from 26 to 28 players the day after this claim, which is why the Yankees, currently holding a ten-game lead over the Baltimore Orioles for the final playoff spot, will not need to drop anyone else to make room for him.

In 2026 disclosures covering his second term, Trump’s accounts executed thousands of trades. Health-care names included:

•  Eli Lilly (purchases totaling as much as ~$680,000 in early 2026), coinciding with administration actions on GLP-1 coverage and manufacturing.
•  West Pharmaceutical Services (injectable-device maker benefiting from GLP-1 demand).
•  Smaller Moderna purchases (tens of thousands of dollars range) later in 2026, plus other names such as Abbott, UnitedHealth, AbbVie, Vertex, Boston Scientific, and Intuitive Surgical. Hundreds of health-care trades were reported in Q1 2026 alone. 

The administration also struck “most-favored-nation” pricing and U.S. manufacturing deals with many large drugmakers (Pfizer, Lilly, Merck, J&J, etc.). Those are policy actions, not personal equity stakes.

Kushner, as a senior White House adviser, coordinated elements of the early COVID response, including PPE and supply efforts, and personally negotiated with Pfizer CEO Albert Bourla for an additional 100 million U.S. doses in late 2020/early 2021. Bourla described the talks as heated, with Kushner taking an “America first” position on delivery timing. 

After leaving office in 2021, Kushner launched Affinity Partners, a Miami private-equity firm. It is funded overwhelmingly (~99%) by Middle Eastern sovereign wealth funds: Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund committed $2 billion early on, with later additions from to roughly $4.8–6+ billion. The firm collects management fees (reported in the tens of millions annually) plus a share of profits. 
Publicly reported Affinity investments include:
•  Phoenix Financial (Israeli insurer; large stake with strong reported returns).
•  Shlomo Group (Israeli car leasing/finance).
•  Revolut (fintech).
•  EGYM (fitness tech) and Whoop (wearable health/fitness).
•  Unybrands (e-commerce aggregator).
•  AI ventures such as Brain Co. (with Elad Gil).
•  Participation in the Electronic Arts take-private.

UAE — biggest by far. The Emirati Genome Programme (Abu Dhabi Dept. of Health with G42/M42) has sequenced more than 900,000 genomes, described by officials as one of the world's most diverse national genomic datasets, with clinical records linked through the Malafi platform and M42 acting as custodian of 3.9 billion health records. The target is one million samples from UAE citizens, collected at 100+ sites with an Emirates ID. A national pharmacogenomics program already runs on the data, letting any physician order a patient's PGx report through Malafi. Officials say the database will soon be opened for research anywhere. 

Bahrain — small but complete. Launched 2019 with a 50,000-citizen sample goal, which was met ahead of schedule. The longer-term plan is 100,000 DNA samples over ten years. Bahrain now offers genome screening through its eGovernment portal and has added newborn genome screening.

Oman — just starting. The Council of Ministers only approved the National Genome and Human Data Centre ("Genome Oman") in January 2025. Worth noting for your purposes: the SQU medical research director framed genetic samples and genomic data as vital national-security content, with the program setting data-security and ethics policies.
